{{about|mathematics|the sports car classification|Group CN|the media group|CN Group|the Canadian corporate group|Canadian National|the cyano-group|cyanide}}
In [[mathematics]], in the area of [[algebra]] known as [[group theory]], a more than fifty-year effort was made to answer a [[conjecture]] of {{harv|Burnside|1911}}: are all [[group (mathematics)|group]]s of [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] [[order (group theory)|order]] [[solvable group|solvable]]? Progress was made by showing that [[CA-group]]s, groups in which the [[centralizer]] of a non-[[identity element|identity]] element is [[abelian group|abelian]], of odd order are solvable {{harv|Suzuki|1957}}. Further progress was made showing that '''CN-groups''', groups in which the centralizer of a non-identity element is [[nilpotent group|nilpotent]], of odd order are solvable {{harv|Feit|Thompson|Hall|1960}}. The complete solution was given in {{harv|Feit|Thompson|1963}}, but further work on CN-groups was done in {{harv|Suzuki|1961}}, giving more detailed information about the structure of these groups. For instance, a non-solvable CN-group ''G'' is such that its [[Core (group)#Solvable radicals|largest solvable normal subgroup]] ''O''<sub>∞</sub>(''G'') is a [[p-group|2-group]], and the [[quotient group|quotient]] is a group of [[parity (mathematics)|even]] order.

==Examples==

Solvable CN groups include
*Nilpotent groups
*[[Frobenius group]]s whose Frobenius complement is nilpotent
*[[3-step group]]s, such as the symmetric group ''S''<sub>4</sub>

Non-solvable CN groups include:
*The [[Suzuki simple group]]s
*The groups PSL<sub>2</sub>('''F'''<sub>2<sup>''n''</sup></sub>) for ''n''>1
*The group PSL<sub>2</sub>('''F'''<sub>''p''</sub>) for ''p''>3 a [[Fermat prime]] or [[Mersenne prime]].
*The group PSL<sub>2</sub>('''F'''<sub>9</sub>)
*The group PSL<sub>3</sub>('''F'''<sub>4</sub>)
